title: Operator-Level Execution Tracing
description: Tracing records every operator's inputs, outputs, shapes, and timing during a model run. The trace reveals exactly what executed in what order, which is the ground truth for debugging. Framework profilers produce these traces natively.

demo.code:
ops = [("matmul", 12.0), ("add", 0.5), ("relu", 1.0)]
for i, (op, ms) in enumerate(ops):
    print("t=%d %s %.1fms" % (i, op, ms))
_jah_schema = {'technique': 'Op tracing', 'trace_target': 'Model run', 'method': 'Profiler hooks', 'output': 'Op timeline', 'benefit': 'Ground-truth execution order', 'complexity': 'Low'}
print("technique:", _jah_schema["technique"])
assert set(_jah_schema) == set(['technique', 'trace_target', 'method', 'output', 'benefit', 'complexity']) and all(_jah_schema.values())
print("schema verified:", len(_jah_schema), "fields")

title: Deterministic Replay from Trace
description: A recorded trace can drive a replay that reproduces the exact execution, inputs included. Replay debugging lets engineers re-run a failure without the original environment. Determinism requires controlling RNG and threading during capture.

demo.code:
trace = {"inputs": [1, 2, 3], "rng_seed": 42, "ops": ["a", "b"]}
print("captured:", trace)
print("replay with seed", trace["rng_seed"], "-> identical outputs")
_jah_schema = {'technique': 'Trace replay', 'trace_target': 'Failing run', 'method': 'Record inputs+RNG', 'output': 'Reproducible run', 'benefit': 'Debug without the original env', 'complexity': 'Medium'}
print("technique:", _jah_schema["technique"])
assert set(_jah_schema) == set(['technique', 'trace_target', 'method', 'output', 'benefit', 'complexity']) and all(_jah_schema.values())
print("schema verified:", len(_jah_schema), "fields")

title: Trace Diffing for Regressions
description: Two traces from different model versions are diffed operator by operator to find what changed. New operators, shape changes, and timing shifts all show up in the diff. This is the fastest way to explain a performance regression.

demo.code:
v1 = ["matmul", "relu", "add"]
v2 = ["matmul", "gelu", "add"]
diff = [(a, b) for a, b in zip(v1, v2) if a != b]
print("v1:", v1)
print("v2:", v2)
print("changed:", diff)

title: Memory Trace Analysis
description: Memory traces record allocations and frees over time, showing the peak and the tensors alive at the peak. The analysis points at the exact tensors to checkpoint or offload. Memory bugs become visible instead of mysterious.

demo.code:
events = [("alloc", "a", 100), ("alloc", "b", 200), ("free", "a", 100), ("alloc", "c", 150)]
live, peak = 0, 0
for op, t, sz in events:
    live += sz if op == "alloc" else -sz
    peak = max(peak, live)
    print(op, t, "live:", live)
print("peak:", peak)

title: NaN Origin Tracing
description: When NaNs appear, the trace is walked backward from the first NaN tensor to find the operator that produced it. Each operator's inputs are checked until the source is found. This turns hours of printf debugging into minutes.

demo.code:
import math
tensors = {"w": 0.5, "x": 1.0, "y": float("nan")}
prod = [k for k, v in tensors.items() if isinstance(v, float) and math.isnan(v)]
print("tensors:", tensors)
print("NaN originates at:", prod)

title: Kernel Launch Tracing
description: Kernel traces show every GPU kernel launch with grid dimensions, shared memory, and duration. They reveal launch overhead problems and underutilized kernels. Optimizers use this trace to pick fusion candidates.

demo.code:
kernels = [("gemm", (128, 1), 12.0), ("relu", (1024, 1), 0.8)]
for name, grid, ms in kernels:
    print("%-6s grid=%s %.1fms" % (name, grid, ms))
print("tiny kernels -> fuse them")

title: Distributed Trace Correlation
description: In multi-GPU training, traces from every rank are correlated by timestamps to show communication stalls. NCCL collectives appear as aligned blocks across ranks. Stragglers stand out immediately in the correlated view.

title: Trace-Based Cost Modeling
description: Historical traces train cost models that predict operator latency from shapes and hardware. The compiler queries the model instead of measuring. Good cost models make auto-scheduling practical.

demo.code:
def predict(m, n, k): return 0.001 * m * n * k / 1e6
for shape in [(512, 512, 512), (1024, 1024, 1024)]:
    print(shape, "-> %.2fms predicted" % predict(*shape))
_jah_schema = {'technique': 'Cost models', 'trace_target': 'Operator latencies', 'method': 'Learned prediction', 'output': 'Latency estimates', 'benefit': 'No measuring needed', 'complexity': 'High'}
print("technique:", _jah_schema["technique"])
assert set(_jah_schema) == set(['technique', 'trace_target', 'method', 'output', 'benefit', 'complexity']) and all(_jah_schema.values())
print("schema verified:", len(_jah_schema), "fields")

title: Execution Verification from Trace
description: A trace is checked against the expected operator sequence to verify the right model actually ran. Mismatches indicate deployment mix-ups. This is a cheap runtime safety check for serving.

demo.code:
expected = ["matmul", "relu", "add"]
actual = ["matmul", "relu", "add"]
print("expected:", expected)
print("actual:  ", actual)
print("verdict:", "MATCH" if expected == actual else "MISMATCH")

title: Gradient Flow Tracing
description: Tracing gradient magnitudes per layer reveals vanishing or exploding gradients during training. The trace shows exactly where the signal dies. Fixes like normalization or scaling target the right layers.

demo.code:
norms = [1.2, 0.9, 0.4, 0.05, 0.001]
for i, n in enumerate(norms):

title: Trace-Driven Test Generation
description: Recorded traces become regression tests: the test replays the trace and asserts identical outputs. Real production traces make the most realistic tests. Regressions are caught by the system's own history.

demo.code:
tests = ["trace_001", "trace_002", "trace_003"]
for t in tests:
    print(t, "replay -> outputs match: True")
print("suite:", len(tests), "tests, all passing")

title: Communication Trace Analysis
description: Collective communication traces show all-reduce sizes, timing, and overlap with compute. The analysis finds bandwidth-bound phases. Overlapping communication with compute is tuned from this data.

demo.code:
comms = [("allreduce", 50, 8.0), ("allreduce", 50, 7.8)]
compute = 7.9
for name, mb, ms in comms:
    print(name, mb, "MB %.1fms overlapped with %.1fms compute" % (ms, compute))

title: Real-Time Trace Monitoring
description: Streaming traces feed live dashboards during training, with alerts on anomalies like NaNs or stalls. Problems are caught in minutes instead of at the end of a run. Monitoring pays for itself with the first saved run.

demo.code:

alerts = [k for k, v in metrics.items() if v is True]
print("metrics:", metrics)
print("alerts:", alerts or "none")

title: Post-Mortem Trace Forensics

title: Trace Privacy Scrubbing
description: Traces can leak training data through recorded activations, so scrubbing redacts values while keeping structure. Scrubbed traces are safe to share with vendors. Privacy and debuggability coexist.
